newsitem.title: USA: Boeing confident on merger despite EC warning.
newsitem.headline: Boeing confident on merger despite EC warning.

text.p: Boeing Co. officials said on Tuesday they were confident of overcoming stiff European resistance to a planned merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp. despite the breakdown of marathon negotiations in Brussels.
"We feel there is still some room for some discussion," Boeing spokeswoman Sherry Nebel said. "We're confident we will reach a mutually acceptable solution."
She and other Boeing officials appeared undisturbed by harsh language from the European Commission staff in Brussels after talks between the two sides ended on Tuesday.
No further talks between the two sides were scheduled, with less than a week before the EC is to make a final decision on the $14 billion deal.

The commission originally had given Boeing a deadline of midnight on Monday Brussels time to alleviate European concerns about the merger's antitrust implications. But when the talks ran on into the night, it pushed the final deadline back a week to July 23, when the commission is scheduled to meet.

Under EU law, the commission has the power to block mergers and takeovers involving companies with a combined worldwide revenue of 5 billion European currency units ($5.5 billion) and 250 million Ecus ($227.5 million) each in sales within the 15-nation bloc.

If Boeing went ahead with the deal regardless of the decision, the commission could fine it up to 10 percent of revenue and also fine any European companies that did business with it. Commission sources said the EU could also seize any new planes being delivered in Europe.
Antitrust lawyers believe Boeing will not run the risk of being shut out of the European market, which accounts for 30 percent of the world's total aircraft orders.

In its strongest language to date, the commission said on Tuesday Boeing had not yet made proposals that sufficiently addressed its fears the merger would harm fair competition for commercial aircraft in the European market.
The commission also formally backed the tough stance taken against the merger by its antitrust chief, Commissioner Karel Van Miert.

"Unless the legitimate competition concerns of the commission can be met and genuine choice maintained for purchasers of aircraft worldwide, the Commission could not approve the merger," commission chief spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas said in a statement that was unprecedented in a merger case.

The statement removed any doubts about the EU's determination to resist warnings from the United States that disapproval of the merger would cause a damaging political fight between the two trade partners.

Boeing officials remained relatively tight-lipped, deflecting questions about the merger even as they led a small group of journalists on a weeklong tour of facilities they hope to acquire in the merger.
Boeing officials said they expected the deal to close on Aug. 1 after shareholders of the two companies ratified it at separate meetings on July 25.

Frank was speaking as antitrust experts from the EU's 15 states met to discuss the $14 billion merger. It followed a warning by the European Commission on Tuesday that it would prohibit the deal unless Boeing made serious concessions.

Brussels-based lawyers, who have been closely watching the fight between the U.S. aircraft giant and the EU, have been speculating that Boeing would improve its offer to avoid the deal being killed altogether. "Nobody completely believes it will be blocked," one said.
National antitrust experts sitting on the EU's advisory committee on mergers and acquisitions unanimously recommended on July 4 that the merger should not be allowed in its current form.

The Commission is expected to give its final ruling on July 23, but left little doubt on Tuesday about its determination to play tough on Boeing by throwing its support behind its competition chief Karel Van Miert -- in what was seen as a repeat performance of next week's meeting.
